tagline: Having an LLM write another model's weights by hand, no gradient descent

scenes.narration: Day 52: Weight-Space Programming has a language model write another model's weights by hand, no gradient descent, MIT licensed.

scenes.heading: What is it?
bullets: The writer designs the architecture itself
scenes.narration: Three frontier LLMs get only ten ARC science questions and write a model's weights by hand. Free to design, they all converge on a sparse fact table read by a fixed procedure.

steps.narration: I took the writer's role myself, reading the same task, and wrote 155 short science facts from memory, nothing from the hidden test set.
Build.py turns each fact into an idf-weighted word vector. Arch.py, a fixed tensor program with no branching, compares each option against every fact by cosine similarity.
The repository's own scorer ran this on the real ARC test set, 3,530 held-out questions, the exact code the paper's authors used.

scenes.heading: What we found
scenes.caption: Chance accuracy versus the hand-written model's real ARC test score (n=3,530).
scenes.narration: A single hand-written pass scored 31.3 percent on the test set, six points above chance, from a weight table where only 2 percent of entries are nonzero.
Full write-up in Japanese on Zenn. Code is MIT licensed, the ARC dataset is CC BY-SA.
